ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਆਧਾਰੁ ਜਨ ਕਾ ਆਸਰਾ ॥:
The devotee takes the Lord’s lotus feet as support and refuge: the beautiful feet are both the concrete image and the spiritual anchor of surrender. It praises divine presence as life’s holding ground, where the humble rest, rely, and find stability instead of worldly attachment (maya).  
Themes: lotus feet, refuge, surrender, divine support, humility, dependence on God, devotion
ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਸੇਵੀ ਰਿਦ ਅੰਤਰਿ ਗੁਰ ਪੂਰੇ ਕੈ ਆਧਾਰਿ: Through grace, keep the beautiful lotus feet in the heart while relying on the Perfect Guru’s shelter; it is a prayer of inward service, meditation, and steady refuge. The lotus feet are the Divine presence, and remembering them within the heart is both loving devotion and surrender. Themes: lotus feet, inner contemplation, refuge in Guru, loving service, grace, simran (loving remembrance), heart-centered devotion
ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਸਿਉ ਪ੍ਰੀਤਿ ਰੀਤਿ ਸੰਤਨ ਮਨਿ ਆਵਏ ਜੀਉ:
The saints keep a settled discipline of loving the Divine’s lotus feet, meaning they hold refuge, devotion, and surrender as their inward habit. The beautiful feet are the image of the Beloved’s presence, and the deeper point is constant attachment to God rather than to maya (worldly attachment); this is the norm that dwells in a saintly mind.  
Themes: lotus feet, divine love, saintly discipline, surrender, refuge, devotion, attachment to God
ਬੋਹਿਥੜਾ ਹਰਿ ਚਰਣ ਮਨ ਚੜਿ ਲੰਘੀਐ ॥:
The mind is urged to board the boat of the Lord’s feet, the image of divine refuge and safe passage, and to cross over the world-ocean. It instructs surrender and trust: by clinging to God’s presence, one is carried beyond maya (worldly attachment) and fear. The concrete boat becomes a spiritual method for reaching the far shore.

Themes: divine refuge, boat metaphor, Lord’s feet, crossing the world-ocean, surrender, liberation, overcoming maya
ਹਰਿ ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਮਨੁ ਬੇਧਿਆ ਕਿਛੁ ਆਨ ਨ ਮੀਠਾ ਰਾਮ:
The mind is pierced and absorbed in the Lord’s lotus feet, an image of loving refuge and intimate union. From that absorption, nothing else in worldly life seems sweet; only the Lord King is प्रिय. It praises the state of single-minded devotion and contempt for all other tastes, with the teeka emphasizing remembrance over every other attraction.  
Themes: lotus feet, pierced mind, loving refuge, divine sweetness, exclusive devotion, simran (loving remembrance), rejection of maya (worldly attachment)
ਪੀ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਆਘਾਨਿਆ ਗੁਰਿ ਅਮਰੁ ਕਰਾਇਆ ॥੨॥: Describes the state of one who drinks the divine nectar and is spiritually satisfied: through the Guru’s grace, the soul is made deathless and beyond decay. The image of drinking and being filled points to inner fulfillment, while immortality and freedom from pain show the result of receiving naam (the divine Name). Themes: ambrosial nectar, spiritual satisfaction, Guru’s grace, immortality, liberation from sorrow, naam, inner fulfillment
ਜਿਨ੍ਹ ਪੀਆ ਸੇ ਮਸਤ ਭਏ ਹੈ ਤੂਟੇ ਬੰਧਨ ਫਾਹੇ ॥:
Those who drink the naam-rasa, the divine Name’s nectar, become intoxicated with spiritual joy; their worldly bonds and nooses are broken. It praises the liberating power of remembrance: tasting the divine sweetness frees the soul from maya (worldly attachment), cutting the chains that bind ordinary life.  

Themes: naam, simran, divine nectar, spiritual intoxication, liberation, breaking bonds, maya, detachment
ਹਰਿ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਸੋ ਚਖੈ ਮੇਰੇ ਮਨਾ ॥੨॥:
Admonishes the mind to seek and taste the Lord’s amrit, the nectar-like naam (divine Name) that gives spiritual life. The image of drinking nectar means inward absorption in remembrance and sustenance from the Divine, not bodily taste. It points to the blessed person who lives by that life-giving water and finds inner vitality through simran.

Themes: naam, amrit, simran, spiritual nourishment, inner life, exhortation to the mind, divine grace
ਹਰਿ ਰਸੁ ਪੀਵਹੁ ਭਾਈ ॥:
Invites the listener, as brothers and companions, to take in the Lord’s nectar, meaning to drink the sweetness of divine remembrance and live by it. The teeka makes this a plea to seek the perfect Guru’s refuge and repeat naam (the divine Name); the image of drinking becomes inward absorption, spiritual nourishment, and surrender.

Themes: naam, simran, divine sweetness, Guru’s refuge, surrender, spiritual nourishment, devotion
ਗੁਰਿ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਹਰਿ ਮੁਖਿ ਚੋਇਆ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਿੰਦੁੜੀ:
The Guru pours amrit, the life-giving naam (divine Name), into the mouth, reviving the soul that was already dying in spiritual death. It praises the Guru as the giver of new life and describes liberation from inner deadness: death is reversed, and the person is made living again by divine grace.  
Themes: Guru’s grace, naam, spiritual rebirth, amrit, inner death and revival, divine life-giving power
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਨਿਧਾਨੁ ਹੈ ਮਿਲਿ ਪੀਵਹੁ ਭਾਈ ॥:
The divine Name is an ambrosial treasure, a spiritual storehouse that gives life and liberation. It urges the listener to join together in sangat and drink this nectar through collective simran, not solitary effort. The image of drinking nectar points to inner nourishment, while the command calls the mind toward shared devotion and surrender to the Divine.

Themes: naam (divine Name), amrit nectar, sangat, simran, spiritual treasure, collective devotion, inner nourishment
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭਉ ਕਟਿਓਨੁ ਫਿਰਿ ਜੋਨਿ ਨ ਪਾਏ ॥:
The Divine cuts away the dread of birth and death, freeing the person from the cycle of rebirth and not sending them back into transmigration. It praises a state of liberation: mortal fear is removed, the round of births ends, and the soul no longer enters another womb.  

Themes: liberation, fear of death, cycle of rebirth, Divine grace, transmigration, salvation
ਸਹਜੁ ਭਇਆ ਪ੍ਰਭੁ ਪਾਇਆ ਜਮ ਕਾ ਭਉ ਲਥਾ ॥੨੦॥:
When the mind settles into सहज poise and steadiness, God is attained; that inner stillness becomes the condition for divine union. With the Lord found, the fear of death falls away, because spiritual death can no longer approach. It is a statement of realized calm, and a reassurance that steadfast remembrance ends terror.  
Themes: intuitive poise, divine union, fear of death, spiritual death, inner stillness, assurance, liberation
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭਉ ਕਟੀਐ ਜਨ ਕਾ ਸਬਦੁ ਜਪਿ ॥:
Birth-and-death fear is cut away by repeating and absorbing the servant’s sacred word of praise; in the company of the devout, this remembrance removes existential dread for a whole lifetime, not just at death. It praises the liberating power of divine praise and presents simran (loving remembrance) as the cure for mortality’s terror.  
Themes: fear of death, birth and rebirth, divine praise, naam (divine Name), simran (loving remembrance), sangat (company of the devout), liberation
ਨ ਦਨੋਤਿ ਜਸਮਰਣੇਨ ਜਨਮ ਜਰਾਧਿ ਮਰਣ ਭਇਅੰ ॥੧॥ ਰ:
Loving remembrance of the Divine, naam (the divine Name), is urged as protection: by simran, the fear and suffering of birth, old age, death, worry, and anxiety do not afflict one. It promises release from the cycle of mortality and inward distress, making remembrance the means of freedom and peace.  
Themes: simran, naam, fear of death, birth and rebirth, old age, liberation, inner peace, anxiety relief
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਦੁਖੁ ਕਾਟੀਐ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਚੂਕੈ ਜਮ ਕੀ ਕਾਣੇ:
Union with the devout company ends the suffering of repeated birth and death and breaks the fear and authority of death. It promises release from the cycle of coming and going, and also instructs the mind that refuge in the sangat can cut life-long sorrow and silence the tyrant of Yama; the teeka stresses this communal cause.  
Themes: repeated birth and death, liberation, deathlessness, fear of Yama, sangat, refuge, ending sorrow
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭੈ ਲਾਥੇ ॥੪॥੨॥੫੨॥:
Birth and death are no longer feared; the mind is relieved of the terror of repeated coming and going. It declares a state of inner freedom, where the cycle of existence no longer terrifies and the self stands beyond dread. The teeka confirms complete removal of this fear rather than a partial easing.

Themes: liberation from fear, birth and death, cycle of rebirth, inner peace, transcendence, detachment
ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ ਕੈ ਆਸਰੈ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਸਿਉ ਰੰਗੁ ਲਾਏ ॥:
Relying on the sangat (company of the devout), one comes to attach love to God and dwell in divine affection. The holy company is both the refuge and the means: by resting in that support, the heart turns from maya (worldly attachment) toward loving remembrance and union, not by self-effort alone but through spiritual companionship.

Themes: sangat, divine love, refuge, devotion, grace, remembrance, turning away from maya
ਸਾਧੂ ਸੰਗਿ ਤਰੀਜੈ ਸਾਗਰੁ ਕਟੀਐ ਜਮ ਕੀ ਫਾਸਾ ਜੀ:
In the company of the holy, one crosses the world-ocean of worldly existence; togetherness with the devout is the means of liberation and the condition for escaping death’s snare. It instructs the seeker to seek sangat (the company of the devout), where the deep sea of maya (worldly attachment) is passed and the noose of judgment is cut away.

Themes: sangat, liberation, world-ocean, death, maya, spiritual refuge, deliverance
ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ ਕੀ ਭੀਰ ਜਉ ਪਾਈ ਤਉ ਨਾਨਕ ਹਰਿ ਸੰਗਿ:
Finding the sangat (the company of the devout) brings union with the Lord; entering that holy gathering leads to meeting God directly. The image of joining the crowded fellowship carries the deeper meaning of grace received, spiritual company, and the end of separation through divine encounter.  
Themes: sangat, holy company, grace, union with God, divine encounter, spiritual companionship
ਸੰਤਤ ਹੀ ਸਤਸੰਗਤਿ ਸੰਗ ਸੁਰੰਗ ਰਤੇ ਜਸੁ ਗਾਵਤ ਹ:
The holy are continuously joined to the sangat (company of the devout), dyed in beautiful divine love, and they sing praise of the Lord. It portrays a steady state of absorption, where loving remembrance and devotion have become natural, and public praise flows from inner union rather than effort.  

Themes: sangat, divine love, praise, absorption, devotion, loving remembrance
ਕਾਢਿ ਲੀਏ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਆਨ ਬਿਖੈ ਤੇ ਸਾਧਸੰਗਿ ਮਨੁ ਲਾਵ:
Pleading to the Divine, the speaker asks to be drawn out of vice, corruption, and sense-pleasures, and to have the mind fixed in sangat, the company of the devout. It is both a rescue and a redirection: removal from maya (worldly attachment) and a turning toward holy company, where the mind becomes steady.  
Themes: plea for deliverance, vice and corruption, maya, sangat, mind discipline, divine guidance, detachment
ਮਹਿਮਾ ਸਾਧੂ ਸੰਗ ਕੀ ਸੁਨਹੁ ਮੇਰੇ ਮੀਤਾ ॥:
Commands attentive listening to the glory of the holy company, addressing companions as friends and urging them to hear carefully. It praises sangat as something exalted and worth taking in with reverence, pointing to the spiritual value of the Guru-centered fellowship itself.  
Themes: sangat, praise, attentive listening, spiritual fellowship, reverence, Guru’s company
ਮੇਰਾ ਗੁਰੁ ਪਰਮੇਸਰੁ ਸੁਖਦਾਈ ॥:
The speaker affirms that the Guru is none other than the Transcendent Lord in living form, the giver of peace and inner comfort. It is praise and confession of refuge: the Guru is not merely a teacher but the source of serenity, the one in whom the seeker rests and from whom all calm arises.

Themes: Guru as Divine presence, refuge and surrender, giver of peace, praise, spiritual comfort
ਤੁਮ ਦਾਤੇ ਤੁਮ ਪੁਰਖ ਬਿਧਾਤੇ ॥:
Addresses the Divine in praise, declaring God as both creator and benefactor: the one who brings beings forth, pervades all, and gives every gift. “Architect of destiny” adds that all fate is ordered by this same power, so the line names dependence on God for existence, blessing, and the shaping of life itself.

Themes: praise, creator, giver, pervading presence, destiny, dependence, divine sovereignty
ਕਰੁਣਾ ਮੈ ਕਿਰਪਾਲ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਨਿਧਿ ਜੀਵਨ ਪਦ ਨਾਨਕ:
Praises the Lord as the source and treasure of mercy, then pleads for darshan, the blessed sight or presence that grants the state of elevated spiritual life and liberation in life. The lotus-like image is refuge and grace, and the speaker asks for direct communion that transforms existence.  
Themes: mercy, compassion, darshan, divine presence, liberation in life, supplication, grace, refuge
ਤੂੰ ਭਾਰੋ ਠਾਕੁਰੁ ਗੁਣੀ ਗਹੇਰਾ ॥੨॥:
Praises the Divine as the great Lord and Master, abundant in virtues and unfathomably deep, and bows into dependence on that excellence. The image of a treasure of qualities and a deep heart both point to overflowing perfection and hidden depth, affirming reverence rather than explanation. It names God as supreme shelter and source of all worthy attributes.

Themes: praise, divine greatness, virtue, depth, lordship, reverence, refuge
ਦੇਵਣਹਾਰੁ ਦਾਤਾਰੁ ਕਿਤੁ ਮੁਖਿ ਸਾਲਾਹੀਐ ॥:
The Great Giver, the generous Lord who gives sustenance to all beings, is beyond full praise; the speaker asks in self-effacing wonder what mouth could ever properly extol Him. It is an act of humility and awe, admitting that divine bounty exceeds all speech, so praise is both due and inadequate.  
Themes: Divine generosity, praise beyond speech, humility, sustenance, human limitation, wonder
ਤੇਰੇ ਕਵਨ ਕਵਨ ਗੁਣ ਕਹਿ ਕਹਿ ਗਾਵਾ ਤੂ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਗ:
The speaker wonders how to even begin praising the Divine, admitting that God’s virtues are countless and beyond full recital. It is an act of awe and worship: the Lord is the master, the treasure-house of all qualities, the sustainer of all. The repeated asking and singing shows praise that can never be exhausted.  
Themes: praise, divine virtues, infinity, lordship, sustainer, humility, devotion
ਰੇ ਬਉਰੇ ਤੁਹਿ ਘਰੀ ਨ ਰਾਖੈ ਕੋਈ ॥:
Admonishes the deluded mind that no one can keep it in the body-home even for a moment; worldly ties offer no refuge and death or departure cannot be delayed. The image of the house points to the human body and transient life, warning against attachment and urging awareness before the brief stay ends.

Themes: deluded mind, body as temporary dwelling, impermanence, mortality, warning against attachment, helplessness of worldly support
ਕਾਹੇ ਮਨ ਤੂ ਡੋਲਤਾ ਹਰਿ ਮਨਸਾ ਪੂਰਣਹਾਰੁ ॥:
The mind is admonished for wavering and urged to stop fear and doubt, because the Lord is the fulfiller of desire and the granter of hopes. It both questions inner instability and reassures with trust in divine completion: the restless mind should rest in the one who satisfies every need.  

Themes: wavering mind, divine fulfillment, hope and desire, inner admonition, trust in God, reassurance, surrender
ਰੇ ਮਨ ਤੂ ਭੀ ਭਜੁ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ॥੨॥:
Admonishes the mind to do devotional remembrance of the Lord of the Universe, not merely hear about Him; the force is urgent self-instruction. “Bhaj” here means active worship, meditation, and loving recollection, so the soul is urged to turn inward to naam (the divine Name) and simran (loving remembrance), making remembrance a lived discipline rather than a passive thought.  
Themes: mind addressed, devotional remembrance, naam, simran, inward discipline, worship, Divine refuge
ਮਨ ਮੇਰਿਆ ਅੰਤਰਿ ਤੇਰੈ ਨਿਧਾਨੁ ਹੈ ਬਾਹਰਿ ਵਸਤੁ:
Admonishes the mind to stop wandering outward for worldly things and recognize that the true treasure, the Divine presence, already dwells within. It contrasts inner spiritual wealth with outer searching in forests and objects, teaching inward turn, self-collection, and finding refuge in what is already present rather than in maya (worldly attachment).  
Themes: mind addressed, inner treasure, Divine presence within, renunciation of outer search, self-inquiry, maya, inward devotion
ਸੁਣਿ ਬਾਵਰੇ ਤੂ ਕਾਏ ਦੇਖਿ ਭੁਲਾਨਾ ॥:
Rebukes the deluded human mind and warns it to listen carefully: why are you lost by looking at maya (worldly attachment)? The image of being mad is a moral diagnosis, not a compliment to worldly sight; seeing the world has led to forgetting the true path. It admonishes, calls for attention, and exposes भ्रम as self-caused wandering.

Themes: admonition to the mind, delusion, maya, worldly attachment, spiritual blindness, warning, lost path, attention to divine guidance
ਸੁਣਿ ਬਾਵਰੇ ਥੀਉ ਰੇਣੁ ਜਿਨੀ ਪ੍ਰਭੁ ਧਿਆਇਆ ॥:
Admonishes the self-lost mind to become the dust of the feet of those who meditate on God, meaning humble service and surrender before the devout are the path to union. The concrete image of dust under feet names radical humility; the deeper point is to erase ego and seek the company of the God-remembrers through simran (loving remembrance).

Themes: humility, surrender, dust under feet, sangat, simran (loving remembrance), ego-loss, union with God
ਲਖ ਖੁਸੀਆ ਪਾਤਿਸਾਹੀਆ ਜੇ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਨਦਰਿ ਕਰੇਇ:
The highest worldly joys, even royal power and countless pleasures, are nothing beside the True Guru’s gracious glance; with that mercy they are counted as already gained. It praises divine favor and teaches that inner fulfillment comes not from status but from being looked upon with grace, as if all kingdoms were received at once.

Themes: grace, True Guru, worldly power, inner fulfillment, divine favor, contentment
ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਹੋਇ ਦਇਆਲੁ ਤਾ ਦੁਖੁ ਨ ਜਾਣੀਐ ॥:
When the True Guru is merciful, suffering is not felt as suffering; divine grace changes the heart so pain loses its sting. It also counsels the seeker that mercy from the Guru transforms hardship into something bearable or even unrecognized, with the teeka stressing that one does not take incoming affliction as real grief.  
Themes: True Guru, mercy, grace, suffering, inner transformation, endurance, painlessness
ਹਰਿ ਚਉਥੜੀ ਲਾਵ ਮਨਿ ਸਹਜੁ ਭਇਆ ਹਰਿ ਪਾਇਆ ਬਲਿ:
The fourth marriage round culminates in union where the mind enters सहज, deep spiritual poise, by the Lord’s grace. It praises the Beloved and states the soul-bride’s surrender: through mercy she finds God and rests in inner steadiness, not merely outward ritual. The image of marriage names spiritual completion, loving union, and calm realization.

Themes: fourth marriage round, spiritual union, divine grace, inner poise, surrender, soul-bride, realization of God
ਸੁਖੁ ਪਾਇਆ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮਨਾਇ ॥:
Pleasing and inwardly enthroning the True Guru brings peace, and the real reward is every desired fruit. The image is of placing the Guru in the heart; the meaning is surrender, devotion, and fulfilled longing. It praises the Guru as the source of contentment and states the result of obedience: calmness, completeness, and spiritual success.

Themes: True Guru, inner devotion, surrender, peace, fulfilled desire, spiritual reward, heart-centered remembrance
ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਸਦਾ ਸਹਾਈ ਜਿਨਿ ਦੁਖ ਕਾ ਕਾਟਿਆ:
The True Guru is declared the speaker’s constant helper and refuge, the one who cuts away the root and banner of suffering for anyone who seeks shelter. It praises steadfast divine support and confesses reliance: pain is not merely eased but uprooted and removed at its source.  
Themes: True Guru, refuge, suffering removed, divine support, surrender, protection, pain uprooted
ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਮਿਲਣ ਕੀ ਇਹ ਤੇਰੀ ਬਰੀਆ ॥:
A direct warning and invitation: this human moment is the appointed chance to meet the Lord of the Universe, so do not waste the present opening for union. It presses urgency and spiritual responsibility, framing life as a rare opportunity for encounter, surrender, and the turn from distraction to the Divine presence.  
Themes: opportunity for union, urgency, human birth, divine encounter, spiritual responsibility, surrender
ਪ੍ਰਾਣੀ ਤੂੰ ਆਇਆ ਲਾਹਾ ਲੈਣਿ ॥:
Addresses the mortal directly and admonishes him to treat human birth as a market for earning the profit of naam (the divine Name), not worldly gain. The arrival into the world is framed as purposeful opportunity: come to collect spiritual benefit, to invest this life in remembrance and return with true gain rather than empty existence.  
Themes: human birth, divine Name, spiritual profit, purpose of life, admonition, worldly market metaphor
ਹਰਿ ਭਗਤਿ ਦ੍ਰਿੜੁ ਮਿਲੁ ਸਾਧ ਨਾਨਕ ਤੇਰੈ ਕਾਮਿ:
Calls the self to meet the holy company and the Guru, and to firmly plant devotion to the Divine in the heart; this is an instruction and warning that only such bhagti (devotional worship) will be useful at death and in life. The lotus-like refuge is inner fixation on the Lord, not outer display, and the teeka stresses making it solid within.

Themes: sangat, Guru, bhagti, inner cultivation, refuge, spiritual usefulness, instruction, warning
ਜੀਵਨਾ ਸਫਲ ਜੀਵਨ ਸੁਨਿ ਹਰਿ ਜਪਿ ਜਪਿ ਸਦ ਜੀਵਨਾ:
Life becomes successful and truly worth living when one hears the divine Name and keeps chanting it in loving remembrance; this is an instruction and praise of the salvific path. Eternal life here means a life aligned with the Lord, not mere bodily continuation, and the emphasis is on hearing, repeating, and abiding in naam (the divine Name).  
Themes: fruitful human life, hearing the divine Name, naam (the divine Name), simran (loving remembrance), spiritual success, eternal living, devotion
ਸੰਤ ਜਨਾ ਕੀ ਰੇਣੁਕਾ ਲੈ ਮਾਥੈ ਲਾਵਉ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ:
Seeking the dust of the feet of the holy, I place it on my forehead as the highest blessing and mark of surrender. The image of dusty feet stands for humility, refuge, and devotion; the teeka expands it into the true treasure beyond worldly riches and powers, greater than the nine treasures and eighteen siddhis.  
Themes: humility, refuge, devotion, saintly company, spiritual treasure, surrender, worldly power rejected
ਗੁਰਸਿਖਾਂ ਕੀ ਹਰਿ ਧੂੜਿ ਦੇਹਿ ਹਮ ਪਾਪੀ ਭੀ ਗਤਿ: Pleading for the dust of the Guru’s Sikhs’ feet, it asks for humble refuge in the sangat (company of the devout). The dust is both a concrete image of service and a means of cleansing the sinner; by contact with saints, fallen beings can gain high spiritual status and release from vice. Themes: humility, sangat, grace, purification, deliverance, sinner’s plea, saintly contact
ਕਰਉ ਨਮਸਕਾਰ ਭਗਤ ਜਨ ਧੂਰਿ ਮੁਖਿ ਲਾਵਉ ॥੩॥:
Bows in reverence to the humble devotees and takes the dust of their feet on the face, a gesture of surrender, humility, and seeking their blessed company. The teeka shifts the stress to joining the sangat (the company of the devout) in singing God’s praises, so the act is both homage and a plea to share in their devotion.

Themes: humility, reverence, sangat, devotion, surrender, blessed company, praise of God
ਟਹਲ ਕਰਉ ਤੇਰੇ ਦਾਸ ਕੀ ਪਗ ਝਾਰਉ ਬਾਲ ॥:
Pleading for the humility of total service, the speaker asks to keep doing the work of the Lord’s servant and to wipe the servant’s feet with one’s hair. The hair-image marks extreme reverence, self-effacement, and surrender: serving the devotee is serving the Divine, and physical care for the holy feet becomes devotion, humility, and blissful obedience.

Themes: humility, service, devotion to sangat, surrender, reverence for holy feet, self-effacement, divine grace
ਕਰਿ ਕਿਰਪਾ ਧੂਰਿ ਦੇਹੁ ਸੰਤਨ ਕੀ ਸੁਖੁ ਨਾਨਕੁ ਇ:
Pleading for divine grace and humility, it asks to be given the dust of the saints’ feet—their humble service, shelter, and purifying contact—as the peace the speaker longs for. The posture is supplication and surrender, seeking inner rest through sangat (the company of the devout) and the lowering of ego before holy feet.

Themes: grace, humility, saints’ dust, refuge, surrender, sangat, peace, ego-lowering
ਸੰਤਹ ਚਰਣ ਹਮਾਰੋ ਮਾਥਾ ਨੈਨ ਦਰਸੁ ਤਨਿ ਧੂਰਿ ਪਰ:
Pleading for total surrender to the holy company: may the forehead rest on the saints’ feet, the eyes remain fixed on their darshan, and the body be covered with the dust of their feet. It asks for constant refuge in sangat (the company of the devout), humility, and lifelong nearness to divine presence through the saints.  
Themes: humility, sangat, darshan, surrender, refuge, devotion, dust of feet
ਅਤਿ ਸੁੰਦਰ ਮਨਮੋਹਨ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਸਭਹੂ ਮਧਿ ਨਿਰਾਰੇ ॥:
Praises the Beloved as supremely beautiful and captivating, present within all yet utterly distinct from all, and turns to that Divine presence in wonder and devotion. The teeka adds that words of praise and glorification give spiritual life, so the line also frames hymns of exaltation as life-giving simran (loving remembrance) and refuge in the divine presence.  
Themes: divine beauty, immanence and transcendence, praise, beloved God, life-giving speech, simran, devotion
ਤੇਰਾ ਨਾਮੁ ਰੂੜੋ ਰੂਪੁ ਰੂੜੋ ਅਤਿ ਰੰਗ ਰੂੜੋ ਮੇ:
Praises the Beloved by repeating beauty in three forms: the divine Name, the divine form/presence, and divine love or color. It is an exclamation of devotion and delight, not argument, gathering all worth into one refuge. The speaker beholds God as utterly lovely and presents simran (loving remembrance) as wonder-filled praise.

Themes: praise, divine beauty, naam (divine Name), divine form, love as radiance, devotion, wonder
ਸੁੰਦਰ ਰਸਾਲ ਤੂ ॥੧॥:
The Divine is praised as beautiful and as the source and reservoir of all sweetness and nectar. It names the Beloved as the fountain of every delight, both lovely in form and the origin of all sustaining rasa, so the speaker is admiring God’s beauty and abundance at once.  

Themes: divine beauty, source of nectar, praise, divine sweetness, abundance, beloved presence
ਨੈਣ ਪਸੰਦੋ ਸੋਇ ਪੇਖਿ ਮੁਸਤਾਕ ਭਈ ॥:
The speaker praises the beloved Divine as lovely to the eyes, then confesses being captivated and intoxicated by beholding that form. The glance at the Lord’s beauty becomes longing and absorption, a state of loving surrender rather than mere sight. The image of pleasing eyes points to inner attraction to the divine presence, and the wording emphasizes enchantment through seeing.

Themes: divine beauty, loving attraction, beholding the Beloved, spiritual intoxication, surrender, longing, divine presence
ਸੁੰਦਰ ਸੋਭਾ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਪਾਲ ਦਇਆਲ ਕੀ ਅਪਰ ਅਪਾਰਾ ਰ:
The beautiful glory of the beloved, merciful Lord of the universe is spreading everywhere, vast and endless. It praises the Divine presence as lovely, compassionate, and beyond measure, with the image of beauty standing for boundless exaltation and all-pervading majesty.  
Themes: divine glory, limitless mercy, all-pervading presence, praise, beauty, infinitude, exaltation
ਅਪੁਨੇ ਸੇਵਕ ਕੀ ਆਪੇ ਰਾਖੈ ਆਪੇ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਾਵੈ ॥:
God preserves his servants everywhere by his own power and keeps their honor intact; he also makes them perform naam (the divine Name) simran (loving remembrance). The line comforts and assures, stressing divine guardianship first, then the grace that turns the servant toward remembrance rather than self-effort.  

Themes: divine protection, preservation of honor, grace, naam, simran, servanthood, remembrance, dependence on God
ਭਗਤ ਜਨਾ ਕੀ ਹਰਿ ਜੀਉ ਰਾਖੈ ਜੁਗਿ ਜੁਗਿ ਰਖਦਾ ਆ:
The Divine preserves the honor and safety of His devotees, and has always done so across ages. It praises steadfast protection, not a one-time rescue, and declares a timeless pattern: the Lord keeps the humble, guards their respect, and maintains the refuge of those devoted to Him.

Themes: divine protection, honor of devotees, timeless mercy, refuge, steadfastness, preservation of dignity
ਭਗਤ ਤੇਰੇ ਸਭਿ ਪ੍ਰਾਣਪਤਿ ਪ੍ਰੀਤਮ ਤੂੰ ਭਗਤਨ ਕਾ:
All devotees are dear to the Lord of life, and the Lord is dear to the devotees; this praises mutual love and belonging, not just divine affection in one direction. The image of “beloved” and “lord of life” joins intimate love with sovereign refuge: the Divine is both cherished presence and the one in whom devotees rest.  

Themes: divine love, mutual devotion, beloved God, refuge, life-giver, intimacy, belonging
ਭਗਤਾ ਕੀ ਟੇਕ ਤੂੰ ਸੰਤਾ ਕੀ ਓਟ ਤੂੰ ਸਚਾ ਸਿਰਜਨ:
The True Creator is praised as the support and refuge of devotees and saints: his naam (divine Name) is their prop, shelter, and place of trust. The image of leaning on him and taking cover in him states surrender, dependence, and steady protection. The teeka stresses that his naam is the actual support and shelter.  
Themes: support, refuge, divine Name, devotees, saints, surrender, protection, trust
ਹਰਿ ਜੁਗੁ ਜੁਗੁ ਭਗਤ ਉਪਾਇਆ ਪੈਜ ਰਖਦਾ ਆਇਆ ਰਾਮ:
God is said to create devotees in every age and to keep protecting their honor, preserving their dignity through all times. The image is of the Lord King raising up the devoted and then standing guard over their prestige; it teaches ongoing divine care, not a one-time act. The focus is assurance and praise of steadfast protection.  
Themes: creation of devotees, divine protection, honor and dignity, timeless care, Lord as sovereign, sustaining the devout
ਹਮਰੇ ਕਰਮ ਨ ਬਿਚਰਹੁ ਠਾਕੁਰ ਤੁਮ੍ਹ ਪੈਜ ਰਖਹੁ ਅ:
Begging the Lord not to judge by past deeds, the speaker pleads for mercy instead of karma, asking the Master to uphold His own honor by protecting the servant’s shame. It is an appeal for grace over merit, a surrender of self-justification, and a request that divine reputation be shown through rescue, not punishment.

Themes: plea for mercy, karma and judgment, divine honor, servant’s protection, grace over merit, surrender, compassion
ਜਾਚਿਕੁ ਮੰਗੈ ਨਿਤ ਨਾਮੁ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਕਰੇ ਕਬੂਲੁ ॥:
The supplicant continually asks for naam (the divine Name), not material gain, and the Lord/Master accepts that prayer. It teaches that true begging is spiritual request, and that persistent simran is granted by divine approval. The image of the beggar and petitioning becomes an instruction in dependence, humility, and the only desire worth asking for.  
Themes: naam, simran, supplication, humility, divine acceptance, spiritual desire, dependence
ਦੇਹਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਸੰਤੋਖੀਆ ਉਤਰੈ ਮਨ ਕੀ ਭੁਖ ॥:
Petition for divine grace: asks for naam (the divine Name) and contentment, so the mind’s hunger, craving, and thirst are ended. The concrete image of appetite is used for inner lack; receiving Naam is both blessing and cure, satisfying desire and settling restless maya (worldly attachment). It is a plea for spiritual fullness and peace.

Themes: supplication, naam, contentment, desire, inner hunger, divine grace, maya, peace
ਜਾਚਿਕੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਾਚੈ ਜਾਚੈ ॥:
The supplicant keeps asking, repeatedly pleading only for naam (the divine Name), making begging itself the action and posture of surrender. It is a humble prayer to the Lord as refuge, owner of all beings, and giver of all comforts; the doubled request stresses persistent simran-like yearning, not material want.  

Themes: begging, naam (divine Name), repeated supplication, surrender, divine refuge, Lord as giver, humility
ਕਰਹੁ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਗੋਪਾਲ ਗੋਬਿਦੇ ਅਪਨਾ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਾਵਹ:
Pleading for divine grace, the speaker asks the World-Sustainer and Lord of the universe to make him recite and remember the divine Name. It is a prayer for inner ability, not mere speech: mercy must turn into naam (the divine Name) chanting and simran (loving remembrance). The pause centers this request as the heart of the appeal, a humble surrender for help in devotion.  
Themes: prayer, mercy, naam, simran, surrender, divine assistance, remembrance
ਜਾਚਕੁ ਮੰਗੈ ਦਾਨੁ ਦੇਹਿ ਪਿਆਰਿਆ ॥:
A supplicant asks for alms from the Beloved, but the gift sought is not wealth: it is divine grace, the endless word, and inward sustenance. The tone is pleading and surrendering, turning hunger into prayer and dependence into loving appeal. The speaker recognizes spiritual poverty and asks to be filled by the Lord’s generosity.  
Themes: supplication, divine grace, spiritual poverty, begging as devotion, inner sustenance, loving address to God
ਦਰਿ ਮੰਗਤੁ ਜਾਚੈ ਦਾਨੁ ਹਰਿ ਦੀਜੈ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਕਰਿ:
A humble beggar stands at the Divine door and pleads for alms, asking for mercy rather than worldly wealth. It is supplication and self-abasement, making the soul dependent on grace: give the gift of favor, grant the charity of the Lord’s kindness, and satisfy need through compassionate giving.  

Themes: supplication, humility, divine mercy, begging at the door, grace as gift, dependence on God
ਮਉਲਿਓ ਮਨੁ ਤਨੁ ਹੋਇਓ ਹਰਿਆ ਏਕ ਬੂੰਦ ਜਿਨਿ ਪਾਈ:
Receiving even one drop of naam (the divine Name) as life-giving nectar makes the mind bloom and the body turn green with spiritual vitality; the image of blossoming and greening stands for inner renewal, joy, and awakening. It praises the smallest contact with divine grace as enough to transform the whole person, not by quantity but by the power of that one drop.  
Themes: naam, divine grace, inner renewal, spiritual vitality, awakening, blessed contact
ਹਰਿ ਰਸੁ ਪੀਵਤ ਸਦ ਹੀ ਰਾਤਾ ॥:
One who drinks the divine nectar of naam (the divine Name) is permanently dyed in it, absorbed in loving remembrance and never separated from that sweetness. The image of drinking holy essence points to inner saturation and lasting spiritual colour, a state of constant immersion rather than a passing taste.  

Themes: divine nectar, naam, simran, spiritual absorption, inner transformation, lasting devotion
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਰਸੁ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਹਰਿ ਗਾਈਐ ਅਹਿਨਿਸਿ ਪੂਰਨ:
Praises and instructs: sing the Lord’s kirtan, the ambrosial nectar of spiritual life, and keep loving remembrance of the Divine day and night. The sacred sound-current fills the inner being continuously, like resonant drums or music sounding without break, producing constant spiritual bliss. This is an exhortation to dwell in divine song until inner consciousness becomes saturated.  
Themes: kirtan, naam, simran, divine bliss, continuous remembrance, spiritual sustenance, inner sound-current
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਰਸਨਾ ਪੀਉ ਪਿਆਰੀ ॥:
Admonishes the beloved tongue, the speaker’s own mind, to drink the ambrosial nectar, meaning to take in naam (the divine Name) as spiritual life-giving sweetness. The image of tasting nectar is both literal devotion and instruction in simran (loving remembrance), urging the mouth to turn from worldly speech to inward nourishment and continual remembrance.  
Themes: tongue, nectar, naam, simran, inward devotion, spiritual nourishment, self-admonition
ਤੇਰਾ ਜਨੁ ਰਾਮ ਰਸਾਇਣਿ ਮਾਤਾ ॥:
Your devotee is drunk with the divine essence of Your naam (the divine Name), absorbed in loving remembrance and carried beyond ordinary sense by that spiritual nectar. It praises a state of blissful intoxication and total immersion in God’s presence; the teeka makes the devotion explicit, while the translation stresses sublime essence.  

Themes: divine intoxication, naam, simran, devotion, absorption, spiritual nectar, bliss
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਰਸੁ ਪੀਆ ਗੁਰ ਸਬਦੀ ਹਮ ਨਾਮ ਵਿਟਹੁ ਕ:
By the Guru’s shabad, the soul drinks the ambrosial nectar of naam (the divine Name), and the speaker offers total surrender, saying he is sacrificed to the Name. It joins instruction and praise: true spiritual life is tasted through the Guru’s word, and the heart responds with devotion, self-offering, and grateful abandon.  
Themes: naam (divine Name), shabad, Guru’s grace, amrit nectar, devotion, surrender, spiritual nourishment
ਰਸੁ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਰਸੁ ਅਤਿ ਭਲਾ ਕਿਤੁ ਬਿਧਿ:
The divine Name as nectar is praised as the highest spiritual essence, life-giving and supremely good. It longs for access to that taste and asks how a person can obtain and inwardly “eat” this sweetness through contact and receptivity. The image is edible relish, but the meaning is the soul’s sustenance and hunger for union with naam (the divine Name).

Themes: naam (the divine Name), amrit (nectar), spiritual sweetness, longing for divine access, inward sustenance, yearning, union
ਬਿਖੈ ਬਨੁ ਫੀਕਾ ਤਿਆਗਿ ਰੀ ਸਖੀਏ ਨਾਮੁ ਮਹਾ ਰਸੁ:
Reject the bland, joyless drink of corruption and sense-indulgence, addressing the soul as a companion and urging it to let go of maya (worldly attachment). Turn instead to naam (the divine Name), the supreme nectar, and keep drinking that sweet, sustaining essence. It admonishes the self to abandon false taste and take refuge in the higher savor of remembrance.

Themes: renunciation, maya, naam, amrit, spiritual sweetness, self-admonition, craving, refuge
ਕਬੀਰ ਬਿਰਹੁ ਭੁਯੰਗਮੁ ਮਨਿ ਬਸੈ ਮੰਤੁ ਨ ਮਾਨੈ ਕ:
Separation from the Divine is pictured as a snake lodged in the mind, a poisonous pain that takes over inward life and will not yield to any charm. The speaker warns that once this anguish of longing or estrangement settles in, no mantra, cure, or worldly remedy can master it; only refuge in the Guru’s shelter is implied as the way beyond it.  
Themes: separation from God, snake image, inner affliction, futility of mantra, longing and pain, Guru’s refuge, mind’s captivity
ਹਰਿ ਬਿਨੁ ਕਿਉ ਜੀਵਾ ਮੇਰੀ ਮਾਈ ॥:
Without the Divine, life is impossible; the speaker pleads to the “mother” address and confesses inner distress. Without naam (the divine Name), the soul is restless and cannot endure, so the line is a cry of dependence, longing, and need for spiritual support rather than a statement about physical survival.  

Themes: dependence on God, longing, naam, inner restlessness, pleading, spiritual survival, devotional lament
ਪ੍ਰਭ ਮਿਲਬੇ ਕਉ ਪ੍ਰੀਤਿ ਮਨਿ ਲਾਗੀ ॥:
Strong love and longing for union with the Divine has taken root in the mind, an inward stirring of devotion rather than a mere feeling. It urges the soul toward meeting, seeking, and surrender. The heart is no longer neutral; it is drawn by loving desire toward God’s presence.  

Themes: longing for union, divine love, inward devotion, seeking the Beloved, surrender, awakened mind
ਹਰਿ ਦਰਸਨ ਕਉ ਮੇਰਾ ਮਨੁ ਬਹੁ ਤਪਤੈ ਜਿਉ ਤ੍ਰਿਖਾ:
The mind burns and longs for the Lord’s darshan, the Blessed sight of the Divine, with the ache of a thirsty person without water. It pleads in yearning, not mere description: inner heat, restlessness, and deprivation show simran’s hunger for presence. The teeka adds the cause as love’s arrow, so the craving is devotion wounded by separation.

Themes: longing for darshan, thirst image, devotional ache, separation from the Divine, simran as hunger, yearning of the mind, love-wound, spiritual restlessness
ਬਾਝਹੁ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਕੋਇ ਨ ਸਾਰੇ ਏਕਲੜੀ ਕੁਰਲਾਏ ॥:
Without the Beloved Lord/Husband, nobody asks after the soul; it laments alone in the world-forest, abandoned and unsupported. The image of solitary crying becomes a plea and confession of helplessness, stressing that only the Divine truly cares, sustains, and answers the soul’s cry.  
Themes: divine intimacy, abandonment, soul’s longing, pleading, world-forest, helplessness, Beloved Lord
ਮਨਿ ਬੈਰਾਗੁ ਭਇਆ ਦਰਸਨੁ ਦੇਖਣੈ ਕਾ ਚਾਉ ॥:
Blessed longing rises in the mind: worldly detachment and love for the Divine drive a desire for darshan, the sight of God’s presence. It praises the state of inward renunciation while yearning for direct vision, treating that yearning itself as spiritual fortune and as the movement of the mind toward the Beloved.

Themes: detachment, longing for darshan, divine love, blessed mind, inward renunciation, spiritual desire, grace
ਘਰਿ ਆਵਹੁ ਚਿਰੀ ਵਿਛੁੰਨਿਆ ਮਿਲੁ ਸਬਦਿ ਗੁਰੂ ਪ੍:
A plea for the Beloved Lord to come dwell in the heart-home and end long separation. The speaker, a soul or bride, asks for union through the Guru’s shabad, seeking inward merging, return, and abiding presence rather than outer arrival. The home image marks the heart as the place of reunion and surrender.  
Themes: longing for union, heart as home, Guru’s shabad, separation and reunion, divine presence, devotional plea, inward merging
ਪਿਰ ਦੋਸੁ ਨਾਹੀ ਸੁਖਹ ਦਾਤੇ ਹਉ ਵਿਛੁੜੀ ਬੁਰਿਆਰ:
The speaker clears the Divine of blame and confesses self-caused separation: the Husband Lord, giver of all peace, is faultless, while her own evil deeds have cut her off. It is an admission of guilt, a pleaful self-reproach, and a reminder that distancing from God comes through one’s own conduct, not divine failure.  
Themes: divine innocence, self-blame, separation from God, sin and consequence, longing for union, moral accountability
ਆਉ ਜੀ ਤੂ ਆਉ ਹਮਾਰੈ ਹਰਿ ਜਸੁ ਸ੍ਰਵਨ ਸੁਨਾਵਨਾ:
An urgent plea invites the beloved Guru/Divine presence to enter the heart-home and dwell there, so the devotee can hear the Lord’s praise with the ears. It is both a request for inner indwelling and an instruction to awaken receptive hearing, making the heart a house for devotional listening and remembrance.  
Themes: supplication, heart-home, divine indwelling, hearing praise, Guru as presence, devotion, receptivity
ਆਉ ਹਮਾਰੈ ਰਾਮ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਜੀਉ ॥:
A loving plea for the Beloved Lord to come and dwell within the heart, not just approach outwardly. The speaker invites intimate divine presence, asking for inner residence, union, and refuge in the heart; the repeated address of “beloved” makes it both a prayer and an expression of longing.  
Themes: divine invitation, inner presence, longing for union, heart as abode, prayer, loving surrender
ਬਿਨਵੰਤਿ ਨਾਨਕ ਦਇਆ ਧਾਰਹੁ ਘਰਿ ਆਵਹੁ ਨਾਹ ਪਿਆਰ:
Nanak pleads for mercy and intimate presence: the Beloved is asked to come home, meaning to enter the heart and dwell within. The image of the returning husband is a prayer for grace, refuge, and union, not mere arrival. It is a humble appeal from the soul to be filled, owned, and brought into inward nearness through divine compassion.  
Themes: plea, mercy, divine indwelling, heart as home, union with Beloved, surrender, longing, simran (loving remembrance)
ਮੋਹਨ ਘਰਿ ਆਵਹੁ ਕਰਉ ਜੋਦਰੀਆ ॥:
Earnest supplication to the आकर्षive Lord to enter the inner house of the heart, not just the outer home: the speaker kneels in humility and begs for divine indwelling. The image of coming into “my house” means taking up residence in the heart through presence, grace, and union. The tone is pleading surrender, a prayer for the beloved God to dwell भीतर and make the soul’s home alive.  
Themes: supplication, divine indwelling, heart as house, humility, longing, union, grace
ਹਮ ਘਰਿ ਸਾਜਨ ਆਏ ॥:
The Beloved Friend, the Lord, has come to dwell in the heart-home, making the inner house blessed and alive. It names a sacred arrival, not ordinary visitors: the Divine is present within, and the soul receives this as intimacy, joy, and fulfilled refuge. The “home” is the heart, and the friends are the Lord’s manifested presence.  
Themes: inner presence, heart as home, divine arrival, intimacy with God, blessed abode, spiritual fulfillment
ਪਹਿਲੈ ਪਹਰੈ ਫੁਲੜਾ ਫਲੁ ਭੀ ਪਛਾ ਰਾਤਿ ॥:
Early devotion is like a flower, and later devotion ripens into fruit; the teeka makes this a praise of worship across the night’s watches, where the first watch is the blossom and the pre-dawn watch yields the true reward. It teaches that steady prayer matures from beauty into fulfillment, from fragrance into nourishment, so early effort becomes ripe spiritual fruit.  
Themes: early devotion, gradual spiritual growth, prayer at night, flower and fruit metaphor, pre-dawn worship, reward of discipline, ripening of meditation
ਕਬੀਰ ਸੂਤਾ ਕਿਆ ਕਰਹਿ ਉਠਿ ਕਿ ਨ ਜਪਹਿ ਮੁਰਾਰਿ:
Admonishes the sleeperly soul, not just physical sleep: why waste life in maya’s spell instead of rising into simran (loving remembrance) of the Divine. The sleeping body is an image of spiritual negligence, while waking means alertness, repentance, and turning toward naam (the divine Name). It warns against squandering human life in forgetfulness and calls for immediate inner awakening.

Themes: spiritual laziness, maya, simran, naam, wakefulness, wasted life, self-admonition, divine remembrance
ਪਰਭਾਤੇ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਿ ਗੁਰ ਕੇ ਚਰਣ ਧਿਆਇ ॥:
At dawn, rise and do naam (the divine Name) simran, fixing the mind on the Guru’s feet as the place of shelter and humble service; the teeka reads this as honoring the Guru who joins one to the Name, not merely visualizing feet. It instructs disciplined early devotion, repeating that remembrance and reverence must begin the day.  
Themes: early-morning devotion, naam simran, Guru’s feet as refuge, humility, disciplined practice, divine remembrance, reverence
ਝਾਲਾਘੇ ਉਠਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਿ ਨਿਸਿ ਬਾਸੁਰ ਆਰਾਧਿ ॥:
Calls the mind to rise early and begin in naam (the divine Name), then keep up simran (loving remembrance) day and night; the point is disciplined, constant devotion, not a single ritual act. It urges waking from laziness and staying absorbed in the Lord at all times. The teeka emphasizes “at ambrosial dawn” and continuous remembrance.

Themes: early rising, naam, simran, constant remembrance, devotional discipline, day and night, spiritual vigilance
ਬਾਬੀਹਾ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲੈ ਬੋਲਿਆ ਤਾਂ ਦਰਿ ਸੁਣੀ ਪ:
The rainbird at the ambrosial hours is an image of the soul crying out in longing; its call becomes prayer, and that prayer is heard at the Divine court. It praises the power of early-morning simran and teaches that earnest supplication in the right hour reaches the Lord; the bird’s cry stands for the seeker’s plea and its answer.  
Themes: rainbird, ambrosial hours, prayer answered, longing of the soul, Divine court, simran, supplication, attentive grace
ਛਾਤੀ ਸੀਤਲ ਮਨੁ ਸੁਖੀ ਛੰਤ ਗੋਬਿਦ ਗੁਨ ਗਾਇ ॥:
Singing the praise of the Lord of the Universe brings coolness to the heart and peace to the mind; the poem asks for, and affirms, inner relief through devotional song. The chest becomes cooled, the mind rests, and simran (loving remembrance) of the Divine settles worldly agitation, replacing distress with calm.  
Themes: praise, devotional song, inner peace, cooling of sorrow, simran, soothing of mind, divine remembrance, emotional relief
ਜੋਗੁ ਬਨਿਆ ਤੇਰਾ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਗਾਈ ॥੧॥:
Singing His praise is presented as the true yoga: by kirtan, the speaker enters spiritual union, gaining the yogic state rather than merely a worldly practice. It praises divine remembrance as the path where both worldly ease and renunciate freedom are found, with praise itself becoming the discipline and the attainment.  
Themes: yoga, kirtan, divine praise, spiritual union, simran, inner fulfillment, renunciation, worldly and spiritual ease
ਹਉ ਅਨਦਿਨੁ ਹਰਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਕਰਉ ॥:
The speaker commits to constant worship: day and night, he keeps doing kirtan, singing praise of the Lord’s naam (divine Name). It is not occasional devotion but nonstop remembrance and adoration, a vow of steady simran (loving remembrance). The same act is named as chanting the Name and offering praise, making remembrance itself the way of life.  
Themes: naam, simran, kirtan, praise, continuous devotion, remembrance, worship
ਰੁਣ ਝੁਣੋ ਸਬਦੁ ਅਨਾਹਦੁ ਨਿਤ ਉਠਿ ਗਾਈਐ ਸੰਤਨ ਕ:
Calls for daily rising early and joining the company of the devout to sing the sweet, resonant, unstruck divine melody of the Word; it is an instruction in disciplined devotion and collective praise. The humming, melodious sound stands for the ever-present spiritual current, and the act of singing with the saints means steady remembrance and worship in sangat, not mere morning ritual.

Themes: early rising, sangat, praise, unstruck sound current, Shabad, disciplined devotion, simran
ਸਾਧੋ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਕੇ ਗੁਨ ਗਾਵਉ ॥:
Calls the saints and mind to keep singing the Lord of the Universe’s virtues continually, making praise into a constant practice rather than a one-time act. It urges loving remembrance through speech, turning devotion toward God’s qualities and away from worldly attachment. The emphasis is persistent worship, ongoing celebration, and disciplined spiritual remembrance.

Themes: praise, continual chanting, divine virtues, simran (loving remembrance), devotional instruction, saints, turning away from maya (worldly attachment)
ਨਿਰਬਾਣ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਗਾਵਹੁ ਕਰਤੇ ਕਾ ਨਿਮਖ ਸਿਮਰਤ ਜ:
Free from desire and attachment, sing the Creator’s praise; make loving remembrance of naam (the divine Name) brief or constant, because even an instant of simran can release one from vice and bondage. The line urges worship as the path out of corruption: praise is not mere song but a saving practice, and inner detachment is both the condition and the result.  
Themes: detachment, kirtan/praise, naam simran, liberation from vice, Creator’s grace, inner purity
ਮਨ ਮੀਠ ਤੁਹਾਰੋ ਕੀਓ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥: The speaker trains the mind to find everything from the Divine sweet, expressing grateful acceptance and loving surrender; the prayer or claim is that no act from that source is bitter. The teeka points instead to a disciplined restraint, that no complaint or reproach has ever been given for any wrong. Themes: acceptance, divine will, sweet to the mind, gratitude, non-complaint, surrender, patience
ਮੀਤ ਕੇ ਕਰਤਬ ਕੁਸਲ ਸਮਾਨਾ ॥੧॥:
The beloved Friend’s doings are accepted as bliss itself; His actions feel beneficial, soothing, and fully good to the speaker. It is not merely approval but surrendering judgment to the Divine will, treating whatever the Lord does as comfort and welfare. The image of friendship carries intimacy, while the deeper meaning is trust in the Creator’s loving order.

Themes: Divine will, acceptance, intimacy with God, trust, contentment, surrender, loving friendship
ਸਰਬ ਸੁਖ ਆਨੰਦ ਮੰਗਲ ਰਸ ਮਾਨਿ ਗੋਬਿੰਦੈ ਆਗਿਓ ॥:
Accepting the Lord of the Universe’s will brings all peace, bliss, joy, and delight; surrender itself becomes the source of sweetness. It praises a state of contentment born from divine resignation, where every experience is turned into comfort. The focus is not on outer gain but on inner release through submission and joyful acceptance.  
Themes: divine will, surrender, contentment, peace, bliss, joy, acceptance, inner sweetness
ਖਿਨ ਮਹਿ ਥਾਪਿ ਉਥਾਪਨਹਾਰਾ ਆਪਨ ਹਾਥਿ ਮਤਾਤ ॥੧॥:
In a single instant, the Divine sets things up and tears them down, creating and destroying by His own power. All decision, control, and final disposal rest in His hands. It warns against human presumption and affirms complete sovereignty: nothing stands by its own strength, and nothing falls outside His command.

Themes: divine sovereignty, creation and destruction, impermanence, divine control, human helplessness, warning against pride
ਨਾਨਕ ਨਾਮੁ ਧਿਆਈਐ ਕਾਰਜੁ ਆਵੈ ਰਾਸਿ ॥੧॥:
Admonishes the mind to keep divine remembrance always present: by meditating on naam (the divine Name) and living in simran (loving remembrance), one’s affairs come to success and every task is put right. The lotus-like focus on the Lord is both inner recollection and practical refuge, a counsel that remembrance clears worldly disorder and makes life’s work prosper.

Themes: naam, simran, remembrance, success, life’s affairs, inner discipline, divine refuge
ਕਾਰਜੁ ਤੇਰਾ ਹੋਵੈ ਪੂਰਾ ਹਰਿ ਹਰਿ ਹਰਿ ਗੁਣ ਗਾਇ:
Commands the mind to keep singing God’s virtues so one’s task is brought to completion and bears sure fruit; the repeated divine name frames praise as the means to success. It is an exhortation to inner devotion, linking remembrance and praise with the fulfillment of life’s work, not mere worldly achievement.  

Themes: praise, mind instructed, divine remembrance, success through devotion, completion of purpose, simran, spiritual fruit
ਨਾਨਕ ਨਾਮੁ ਅਰਾਧਣਾ ਕਾਰਜੁ ਆਵੈ ਰਾਸਿ ॥੮॥:
Loving remembrance of naam (the divine Name) is urged as the true task, and it brings one’s affairs to completion; the world’s business, life’s purpose, and inner work all come to success through simran. It both instructs the mind to dwell on God and promises that surrendering to that focus makes everything turn out right.

Themes: naam, simran, success, life purpose, divine guidance, completion, spiritual practice
ਸਭੇ ਕਾਜ ਸਵਾਰਿਐ ਜਾ ਤੁਧੁ ਭਾਵੰਦਾ ॥੭॥:
All affairs are set right when the Divine is pleased; the speaker states dependence on divine will and thanks or pleads for grace. The image is of every task being smoothed and completed, but the deeper point is surrender: only when God’s will is accepted do worldly matters fall into order and succeed.  
Themes: divine pleasure, surrender to hukam, life’s affairs resolved, grace, dependence on God, worldly success through divine will
ਸਗਲ ਮਨੋਰਥ ਪੂਰਨ ਹੋਏ ਕਦੇ ਨ ਹੋਇ ਦੁਖਾਲਾ ਜੀਉ:
All wishes and needs are fulfilled, and sorrow is absent; the stance is a declaration of blessed completion and freedom from suffering. It points to a state where every purpose is met, every lack removed, and grief no longer reaches the one who has attained divine grace. The sense is not mere success but lasting wholeness, inner satisfaction, and release from pain.  
Themes: fulfilled desire, freedom from sorrow, divine grace, completeness, contentment, inner peace, liberation from suffering
